rows.q: What does Katz mean by imperative exchange?
rows.a:
"Imperative exchange" is Katz's name for the oldest and most stubborn way humans relate to the **center**: the shared focus around which a community forms, and for Katz the source of every command it obeys. The idea is simple. The center commands, we obey, and in obeying we issue a command of our own back to it. The trouble lies in what happens when the center doesn't keep its side.

## The basic structure: ritual as a two-way command

You need one piece of Katz's "originary grammar" to follow this. He distinguishes the *ostensive* (pointing: "that!"), the *imperative* (a command or request: "bring that!") and the *declarative* (a sentence that describes things as they are). Imperative exchange belongs to the world of imperatives, before the declarative takes over.

His clearest example is sacrifice:

> "Sacrifice involves an imperative exchange because the human member of the community offering the sacrifice (bringing his goat, or whatever, to the altar) is following an order issued by the deity to offer up some of the fruits provided, ultimately, by that deity; while, in exchange, the sacrifice represents a request, on the part of the one offering the sacrifice, that the deity continue providing these benefits (more goats)." ([Beyond "Post-Sacrificial"](/post/beyond-post-sacrificial#p-1))

The exchange is lopsided. Elsewhere he calls ritual "an asymmetrical imperative exchange": "the participant fulfills some command of the center while making a request of the center" ([Languaging Practices](/post/languaging-practices#p-2)). The center gave first and gave everything, and the worshipper returns a portion and asks for more.

The idea comes from the originary scene itself. There the central object "says" only one thing: *don't grab*. Once the community has eaten the object and the center outlasts it, the center "now receives imperatives along with issuing them, and is therefore increasingly defined by this dialogue with the community" ([The Discourse of the Center](/post/the-discourse-of-the-center#p-3)). Katz also describes the exchange as an attempt at repair: it "results from ostensive failure, and aims at restoring an ostensive relation to the center" ([Ostensive-Imperative Generativity and Scenic Design Practices](/post/ostensive-imperative-generativity-and-scenic-design-practices#p-3)). We no longer simply stand before the center pointing; we have to petition it to show up again, in the form of the next meal or the next good harvest.

## When the exchange fails: myth, the declarative, resentment

The center does not always deliver, and most of the concept's force comes from this. When the rain doesn't come, someone has to explain why, and the explanation is myth. Ritual was performed wrongly, or the god has other purposes. Katz gives this as one of the jobs of the declarative sentence in its early life: "to supplement a failed imperative with a 'real' that preserves the relations implicit in the failed imperative" ([Languaging Practices](/post/languaging-practices#p-2)).

He makes a stronger claim about thinking itself:

> "Thinking begins with the failure of some imperative exchange—I did this, but reality didn't supply that, and why in the world should I have expected it to, since it's not subject to my commands or tied to me by any promise. The declarative sentence, then, is best understood as the conversion of a failed imperative exchange into a constraint." ([Cognition as Originary Memory](/post/cognition-as-originary-memory#p-25))

On this account the declarative, our whole apparatus of facts and descriptions, grows out of disappointed bargains with the center.

A failed exchange can also simply persist as a grievance, and that is how Katz defines **resentment**: "your fulfilling of an imperative, having the reciprocal imperative you issue go unfulfilled, while not letting that reciprocal imperative lapse" ([Resentment](/post/resentment#p-19)). Resentment is an imperative exchange you refuse to close. The same essay supplies the way out: let the reciprocal imperative lapse, or turn the demand into a question.

## Why it escalates, and how it gets broken

Imperative exchange tends to inflate. The more the center is credited with giving, the more it seems to demand back, until "in the end, the most treasured possession, i.e., your first born" ([The Sovereign Remembering of Names](/post/the-sovereign-remembering-of-names#p-8)). Katz ties this to human sacrifice and to divine kingship. If the king or god has given you everything, no goat can repay it.

The break, which Katz takes from Gans's reading of the burning bush in *Science and Faith*, works by demanding more instead of less. The God whose name is a declarative sentence ("I AM THAT I AM") cannot be bargained with:

> "since God has given everything to you, you are to give everything to God... There is no more commensurability and therefore no more exchange." ([Cognition as Originary Memory](/post/cognition-as-originary-memory#p-24))

This is what Katz means by "post-sacrificial." The question changes from "how do we get what we're owed" to "what makes you think obligations can be calculated?" ([Beyond "Post-Sacrificial"](/post/beyond-post-sacrificial#p-15)). He calls the resulting condition "interrogative imperativity": you are still under command, but now you are asking how to serve rather than negotiating terms.

## It never goes away

Katz insists that imperative exchange "cannot be eliminated—it is embedded in our habits, it is the form in which we remember the sign and forget the scene—if I do this, reality will supply that" ([Cognition as Originary Memory](/post/cognition-as-originary-memory#p-25)). Modern secular life is full of it. "Play by the rules and you'll be rewarded" is a prayer to institutions. The task is to keep testing these exchanges: "Declaratives essentially demystify these little imperative exchanges we live by... But even that involves following an imperative: keep testing those imperative exchanges" ([Sovereign Commands, Anarchistic Demands](/post/sovereign-commands-anarchistic-demands-gablog#p-15)).

The exchange can also be refined instead of abolished. Its purest form is prayer:

> "A prayer involves an exchange of imperatives: tell me how to serve you. At its most refined, or most 'technical,' the imperative exchange enacted in prayer distills itself into something like 'help me to know how to donate to you.'" ([Mimesis, the Center and Auto-Immunology](/post/mimesis-center-auto-immunology#p-40))

This is the root of a recurring formula in Katz's later work, "donate your resentment to the center." You stop demanding payment and ask instead for clearer commands.

## Where the concept goes in the recent work

In the recent Substack essays imperative exchange becomes central again, now joined to technology, which Katz defines as "perfecting the imperative." He calls imperative exchange "an extremely important concept for center study," a space "where the unarticulated interfaces with the articulated," before the declarative ([Perfecting the Imperative and Imperative Exchange: Originary FinTech](/post/perfecting-the-imperative-and-imperative-exchange-originary-fintech#p-1)). He sees it splitting two ways. One branch keeps perfecting the imperative, which is technology: commands built into machines so that they are fulfilled reliably. The other "solicits the nomos," the original distribution of property and credit from the center ([same essay](/post/perfecting-the-imperative-and-imperative-exchange-originary-fintech#p-18)). So money, credit and technology are later forms of the bargain the worshipper struck at the altar. In this phase he describes the relation as "decidedly asymmetrical: petition meeting command" ([Media, Technology and Originary Grammar](/post/media-technology-and-originary-grammar#p-19)).

## Applying it

Take a student who does every assignment and expects a good job at the end. That is an imperative exchange: the institution commands ("study, comply"), and the compliance carries a demand of its own ("now reward me"). If the job doesn't come, Katz's analysis lays out the options. The student can keep the demand open, which is resentment. He can build a myth about who cheated him, which tends to look for a scapegoat. Or he can let the bargain fail and turn it into a question and then a constraint: what did I actually assume about how credentials work, and what does the center (the economy, the profession) now require of me? Only the last option produces knowledge. In its most refined form it becomes something close to prayer: show me how I'm actually needed.

## What to read next

- [Beyond "Post-Sacrificial"](/post/beyond-post-sacrificial) has Katz's clearest account of how sacrifice embodies imperative exchange and what replaces it.
- [Cognition as Originary Memory](/post/cognition-as-originary-memory) connects the concept to the birth of the declarative sentence and to thinking itself.
- [Perfecting the Imperative and Imperative Exchange: Originary FinTech](/post/perfecting-the-imperative-and-imperative-exchange-originary-fintech) shows where Katz has taken it lately, into technology, credit and money.

An exercise: pick one "if I do this, I'll get that" you live by, at work, in a relationship or as a citizen. Write it out as two imperatives, the one you obey and the one you silently issue back. Then ask what declarative sentence you would have to accept if the second imperative were never honored.

rows.a:
**Short answer: no. Katz's answer, though, is closer to "no, and yet nearly."** He puts it this way:

> "I do have to acknowledge that GA is odd in being very similar to a religion and at the same time the exact opposite of one." ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-4))

GA (Generative Anthropology) is the field Center Study grew out of.

## Why it looks like a religion

At its root is an origin story: the *originary scene*. A group of proto-humans converges on a shared object, and violence breaks out or is about to. One gesture of reaching is held back and becomes a sign, others imitate it, and the crisis is *deferred*. On this account, the first sign, the first human community and the first sacred object come into being at once.

A story about how humans, language and the sacred began has the shape of a myth. That is also why the human sciences avoid the question altogether: "Thinking in terms of origins marks one as introducing theology into rational discussions" ([Lecture 1: Origin](/post/origin#p-1)).

Katz also admits that accepting the hypothesis feels like converting. "Something like a conversion experience may be necessary here: you'd have to be able to abandon and revise all 'priors'" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-6)).

## Why it is the opposite of a religion

The hypothesis does not belong to any faith. It claims to explain where faith comes from. Center Study is "the antithesis of faith and religion by disclosing the originary possibility of all faiths and religions" ([Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-1)).

Three differences follow from this.

- **It asks for no belief in the usual sense.** It is a hypothesis: "I don't see it as a question of 'belief' (which I don't 'believe' in), but it does, perhaps, require a willingness to live or think in a kind of 'suspense'" ([source](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-4)).
- **It offers no salvation and no rite.** Katz asks why anyone would "go off into the wilderness with a hypothesis which acknowledges it can never be proven, and doesn't promise salvation?" ([source](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-6)). He contrasts this with the followers of René Girard, who can build a community around exposing scapegoating. Center Study has no founding event of its own that a community could gather to repeat ([p-9–10](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-9)).
- **It doubts the word "religion" itself.** Katz notes there is "no single phenomenon called 'religion' that includes all the practices" studied under that name. He also notes that the category itself "is modeled on Protestantism" ([Generative Anthropology as the One Big Discipline](/post/generative-anthropology-one-big-discipline#p-32)). He would sooner use a more minimal word: "We get much closer to minimality with a word like 'commemoration'" ([Inscription](/post/inscription#p-3)).

## Where it stands toward actual religions

Center Study does not side with Enlightenment debunking. Katz writes that "the faiths are truer than philosophy, and it's not even close" ([Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-2)). The religions have been working with the center and the deferral of violence all along, while philosophy has tried to step outside the scene.

Still, the hypothesis cannot simply sit alongside a faith on equal terms. If you take it literally, "you can only see your faith tradition as an approximation of a configuration you consider prior and irreducible to that tradition" ([p-1](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-1)). A later essay is gentler: "Historic faiths are discovery procedures whose results can be assessed while being maintained as ongoing inquiries." The hypothesis then serves as "a kind of meta-faith" ([Deferral and Appropriation; Property and the Center](/post/deferral-and-appropriation-property-and-the-center#p-2)).

So if there is a faith here, its object is not a deity. It is the ongoing life of the scene itself: "that there will always be new things at the center to draw forth further signs and scenes from us" ([Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-14)). Elsewhere Katz says that if pressed on what he believes, his answer is "language" ([Compression](/post/compression#p-10)).

## Next reading

- [The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself) is Katz's most direct account of why the hypothesis feels like a faith and why it is not one.
- [Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip) describes how Center Study stands at once "closest and furthest from any faith tradition."

May I ask what prompted the question? Are you coming from a religious tradition and wondering whether this competes with it? Or does Center Study strike you as a secular theory dressed in religious language? The answer would go in a different direction for each.

rows.q: What is thirdness in Katz's recent essays?
rows.a:
In the recent essays, from roughly 2023 on, "Thirdness" means two things that Katz deliberately keeps together. It is the name of a company he proposes, and it is a way of thinking that the company is meant to train. To see why he wants them fused, it helps to start with the name and then follow the project as it develops.

## Where the name comes from

Katz explains the title directly: "Thirdness (a reference to Washington's third man as well as Peirce's concept of generality and significance created through agreement)" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-22)). The "third man" comes from George Washington's will, which Katz quotes. Disputes over the will are to be settled by three impartial men, two of them chosen by the disputants and the third chosen by those two, who "shall, unfettered by law, or legal constructions, declare their sense of the Testator's intention" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-8)). So the core figure is the impartial third party who stands between two claimants. That party is bound less by legal technicality than by a "sense" of the juridical itself.

The word has an older history in his writing. Around 2015, drawing on Peirce, he described thirdness as "the recipient and normalization of the interplay of firstness and secondness," and also as "the position of the witness or spectator," the ability to step back far enough from events "to observe them as an unfolding drama," which he calls "an originary source of thinking, morality and esthetics" ([The Single Source of Moral and Intellectual Innovation](/post/the-single-source-of-moral-and-intellectual-innovation-gablog#p-11)). In the same period he argued that "Civilization depends upon deferral to the judgment of the 'third person'" and upon everyone taking on that person's dispositions ([Flouting Civilization](/post/flouting-civilization#p-11)). The recent Thirdness turns that disposition into an institution.

## The starting premise: the juridical

The project rests on Katz's emphasis on the *juridical*, his term for the sphere of courts, claims and judgment. He places it between ritual on one side and the disciplines (organized inquiry) on the other. Its job is to lift conflicts out of the vendetta, the cycle of revenge, by bringing them before a third party who can enforce a decision. It must also stop the legal system itself from becoming a weapon against the basic order of property and authority. His strongest claim is that "nothing 'happens' that could not be framed as including potential claimants before some tribunal" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-1)). On this view, to understand any event, a war for example, is to "sort out claims and counter-claims the respective sides do and might make against each other and the kind of tribunal that might sit in judgment" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-4)).

## How the project develops

The proposal goes through stages, and the essays let you watch it change.

1. **A journal.** At first Thirdness was to publish essays that frame events as hypothetical cases. The quality of those analyses would then make its writers credible as a real arbitration firm. Parties with honest disputes would want it, and anyone "interested in honing grudges for the sake of institutional blackmail would avoid the firm like the plague" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-6)).

2. **A prediction market.** Then the turning point: "The notion of a prediction market then presented itself" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-11)). People can bet reliably only on events that have an agreed closure, such as games or elections. If a trusted team constitutes events *as cases* and issues judgments on them, then any event becomes something people can bet on. You are not betting on the event itself so much as "on the judgment rendered" ([Thirdness](/post/thirdness#p-14)). The team frames each case as close to 50/50 as it can, so that, like a bookie, it simply takes the vig. Bettors who get good at anticipating the team's reasoning are, in practice, being trained in juridical thinking, and the best of them should be recruited ([Modeling Thirdness](/post/modeling-thirdness#p-13)).

3. **Data exchange instead of punishment.** In *Modeling Thirdness* the deeper aim is spelled out: "The political project advanced by Thirdness is to transition the juridical... into data exchange... each party donating and/or receiving data from the center in lieu of such things as punishment or damages" ([Modeling Thirdness](/post/modeling-thirdness#p-2)). A settlement then means something like this: "To settle a case is to have each side know something about the other side's likely future actions that they didn't before" ([Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence#p-23)). Policy itself starts to look like "proposed modifications in the Stack" (Katz's word for the global layering of computational infrastructure), and his summary is: "The irreducibility of the juridical, the question of justice... serving as the mode of measurement of data security and exchange—that's Thirdness" ([Modeling Thirdness](/post/modeling-thirdness#p-20)).

4. **Currency and idioms.** Finally, the judgments and the language they produce become a medium of exchange. The language of a good settlement would be adopted into the public documents of teams, and "Currency can be eliminated from the settlement insofar as the settlement itself becomes currency" ([Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence#p-25)). The bettor's reasoning paths can be "mined" as idioms, reusable phrasings that carry the logic of a case ([Mining Idioms in Thirdness](/post/mining-idioms-in-thirdness#p-12)). Thirdness "aspires to become the world company" ([Mining Idioms in Thirdness](/post/mining-idioms-in-thirdness#p-7)), and it is one route toward *learncoin*, his name for pedagogy that functions as currency ([Learncoin](/post/learncoin#p-10)).

## The 50/50 as a way of thinking

The essays also extract a habit of mind from the betting mechanism. If cases are built to sit at 50/50, then you can approach *any* topic by looking for its 50/50 point: "speak only of the 50/50, and continue your discourse by spreading the 50/50 through all the implications" ([Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence#p-2)). The idea is to turn away from the "majority take" questions, such as whether someone is guilty. Instead you look for questions on which no majority could form, because they exist only "as an especially good occasion to exercise specific forms of judgment" ([The Same Sentence](/post/the-same-sentence#p-16)). The point of all this, in Katz's words, is "to use the concept of justice to systematically take the temperature of institutions."

## The paradox at the end

Katz keeps saying that the perfection of the juridical would be its abolition. If capture and adjudication became certain, there would be nothing left to try. Thirdness has the same structure. In the last analysis you would be "betting on which decision the Thirdness team deems more likely to increase the likelihood, albeit asymptotic, that Thirdness will be abolished as it is taken up in all everyday practices" ([If… Then](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-23)). Thirdness aims to make itself unnecessary by turning everyone into the impartial third.

## Applying it

Katz's own examples show how this works. Take a confrontation between protesters and a police officer and treat it as two suits against each other. The protesters are asked to supply "a theory of justice and the state to justify their actions," and the officer is asked what "resource from his training and experience he might have drawn upon in controlling the protesters more effectively" ([If… Then](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-19)). The question is not who is right in general. It is whether the officer embodied "a mode of authority" that someone in that situation was obliged to respect. A question framed that way is genuinely uncertain, and so it is worth betting on and worth thinking about.

He is also frank about the practical state of things: for now, Thirdness "does probably need first of all to be a more conventional online journal," closer to an academy training a "new officer class" than to a consulting firm ([Modeling Thirdness 2](/post/modeling-thirdness-2#p-16)).

## What to read next

- [Thirdness](/post/thirdness), the founding proposal, in which you can watch the idea grow from journal to market to "world brain."
- [Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence), the most explicit on the 50/50 as a method of thinking and on settlements becoming currency.

An exercise: pick a dispute in today's news and, instead of asking who is right, build a narrower case around it that a trained team could reasonably split 50/50 on. Katz suggests one such move, asking whether a media outlet will correct a particular claim instead of whether a defendant will be convicted ([Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence#p-4)). Then notice how much you had to take as settled before the 50/50 could appear at all. Katz returns again and again to that set of assumptions in the background.

rows.q: How would Center Study read a social media pile-on?
rows.a:
## The pile-on as a small originary scene going wrong

Center Study would read a pile-on as the human scene in miniature, run in the wrong direction. Katz uses almost this exact case to define the central term:

> "The center is whatever interferes with violent centralization. Think about it this way: have you ever felt (and given into) the temptation to 'pile on' someone who is being criticized, attacked, or ridiculed? There is no way you would have been thinking of the clever bon mot you are about to add without the mimetic instigation of those who have already dropped a couple." ([Revivalistics](/post/revivalistics#p-1))

Some vocabulary first. In the originary hypothesis, a group converging on one object is stopped short by a gesture that defers appropriation. That gesture is the first sign, and the object becomes a *center*: something everyone attends to without seizing. *Violent centralization* is the opposite movement. Attention converges on a figure in order to seize, expel or destroy it.

A pile-on is that convergence made visible. Each reply is mimetic, because you only thought of your quip after seeing the others. Each reply also accelerates the convergence instead of interrupting it. The person being piled on becomes the "center" in the bad sense: the target of everyone's attention, not a figure everyone holds off from.

## A trial without a court

Katz's second move is to read social media as a kind of ritual court:

> "The mass media, and now social media, do perpetually position us as judges on events involving some purported transgression, commanding us to 'take a position' and add our little quantum of power to whatever target is being displayed on the Big Scene (and Big Screen)." ([Media as Ritual](/post/media-as-ritual#p-1))

He also writes: "All the media does is stage trials and invite the audience to participate vicariously as judges, jurors and, increasingly, enforcers" ([Media as Infrastructural Translation](/post/media-as-infrastructural-translation#p-13)). Each of us is on "perpetual 'call' to add one's own voice in judgment to the crowd directed at the target of the day—but also in terms of the intense desire to be exempt from that judgment" ([same text](/post/media-as-infrastructural-translation#p-10)).

That last clause is the mimetic engine. Joining the crowd is the surest way of not being its next target.

This is why Katz cares so much about the *juridical*. A court turns a potential vendetta into a structured dispute, with standing, evidence and a judge. A pile-on uses the vocabulary of justice ("racist," "fraud," "harm") without any of those forms, so it is the vendetta wearing the court's clothes.

He also says that "Scapegoating is also always against the center... The claim implicit in scapegoating is that the center has been usurped by someone 'behind the scenes'" ([Bouvard on Scapegoating and Egalitarian Morality](/post/the-egalitarian-vs-hierarchical-model-of-morality#p-1)). The crowd acts as though legitimate authority has failed to deal with this person, so it appoints itself.

## Not just "retribalization"

You might reach for the familiar account that social media returns us to tribal orality. Katz rejects this as "a consumerist approach to the question" that "leaves the Stack out of account" ([The Sentence as Metric](/post/the-sentence-as-metric#p-1)). The *Stack* is his name for the layered infrastructure of platforms, algorithms and data that scenes now run on.

Looking at a reply thread on X, he suggests that "maybe the entire reply section is a sentence; maybe this reply section is itself a verb or expletive in a much longer sentence including many reply sections, the bot farms and algorithms producing them, resentments amplified by those algorithms" ([Media, Technology and Originary Grammar](/post/media-technology-and-originary-grammar#p-9)).

So a full reading asks two questions:
- What are the people doing?
- How is the scene *designed*? What gets amplified, who benefits, and what does the pile-on feed upstream?

## Where the line falls, and what to do

Katz doesn't let this collapse into "never criticize anyone." The same passage asks what kind of concentrated focus would not be violent centralization, since "We must be permitted condemnation of wrong actions, sharp and uncompromising critiques... the conviction and punishment of criminals" ([Revivalistics](/post/revivalistics#p-1)). His answers run along three lines.

**1. Move it into juridical form.** His most pointed proposal is to make defamation law robust. You should be able to sue someone who calls you "racist" without a coherent definition and an account of how it applies ([Nomos/Class Action](/post/nomos-class-action#p-7)). If that happened, "Wars on social media would be transformed from exchanges of insults and spite into evidence collection missions" ([p-10](/post/nomos-class-action#p-10)).

**2. Design, don't just denounce.** "A lot of scapegoating takes place on social media—at times it seems like little else goes on there." The task is to use it "to design social interactions or 'interfaces' that foreground dangerous markings along with ways of deferring their danger" ([Design and the Attentional Economy](/post/design-and-the-attentional-economy#p-14)).

**3. Watch your own position on the scene.** This is the most practical point. "Putting someone else at the center implies the possibility of being placed in the center yourself in turn." If you attack, "know that you're going to been seen, red in tooth and claw, knives out." Katz offers a rule of thumb: "let all your utterances (samples) be as close to 50% directing attention to the other and 50% drawing attention to yourself as possible" ([Idiom and the differend](/post/idiom-and-the-differend#p-15)). He calls this *originary satire*. You expose the grabbing for the center, including your own, until the exposure becomes "a prelude and invitation" to deferral ([p-14](/post/idiom-and-the-differend#p-14)).

This is "reading the room" in his sense, which "involves getting a read on others reading of you" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-53)).

## Applied to a case

Suppose someone posts a clumsy joke, and quote-tweets begin calling them a bigot. A Center Study reading would ask four things in turn:

1. **The mimetic step.** Which replies merely repeat earlier replies, and how fast is the convergence accelerating?
2. **The missing juridical form.** What precise charge, by what standard, would hold up as a claim? Usually none would. That gap is the sign of a vendetta.
3. **The Stack.** What is being amplified, and by what? The answer may include bots.
4. **Your own gesture.** Katz names the options himself: reply "trying to short-circuit the sequence," or stay out and let the sameness of the replies expose itself ([Media, Technology and Originary Grammar](/post/media-technology-and-originary-grammar#p-10)).

Whatever you do, he insists on one thing: "What it is imperative to resist... is the desire to destroy, engulf, incinerate, the figure you see at the center" ([Media as Ritual](/post/media-as-ritual#p-16)).

## Further reading

- [Media as Infrastructural Translation](/post/media-as-infrastructural-translation) is Katz's fullest account of media as staged trials, and of what replacing them would look like.
- [Idiom and the differend](/post/idiom-and-the-differend) works out the 50/50 rule and originary satire against the Jewish tradition of *lashon hara*, the prohibition on harmful speech about others.

An exercise: take a recent pile-on you watched. Write the reply you were tempted to post. Then rewrite it so that half its attention falls on what *you* wanted from joining in. Does it still read as a pile-on?

rows.q: What does Center Study suggest about how to write a good prompt for an AI?
rows.a:
Katz never writes a how-to guide for prompting. He does return to prompting often, though, because for him it is an unusually clear instance of something humans have always done. Taken together, those passages amount to a fairly definite account of what makes a prompt good. I'll build it up in four steps and then apply it to an example.

## 1. A prompt is a request addressed to the center

In Katz's terms, everything we do takes the form of an *imperative exchange* with the center: we obey what it asks of us and ask it in return for guidance. The model for this is prayer. He places prompting directly in that lineage. Learning, he writes, has always been a matter of drawing imperatives out of the center, "whether this is done by more rehearsal of a chant and dance or by revising a prompt or search term eliciting information from the center is the aim" ([Nomos and Transfer Translation](/post/nomos-and-transfer-translation#p-20)).

This changes what counts as success. A prompt is not a command fired at a tool that should return a finished product. It is one turn in a continuing exchange, and the exchange refines you as much as it refines the output. Hence his definition of prompt engineering as "the designing of search terms that would elicit results from searches into textual databases (i.e., AI) that will most powerfully suggest the design of a new search term" ([Techno-Grammar](/post/techno-grammar#p-1)).

So the first criterion is this: **a good prompt is judged partly by the next prompt it makes possible.** A prompt that returns an answer and leaves you with nothing further to ask has, by this standard, done poorly.

## 2. The grammar of a prompt: imperative, then question, then statement

Katz's *originary grammar* follows how speech forms grow out of one another. Pointing (the ostensive) leads to commanding (the imperative). An imperative that cannot be met is drawn out into a question (the interrogative). The question finally settles into a statement about how things are (the declarative). He applies this sequence to AI directly: the search is conducted "by giving the 'AI' ... imperatives and asking it questions," and "those imperatives that can make the trek through to the declarative will be 'selected for'" ([Techno-Grammar](/post/techno-grammar#p-11)).

In practice, a prompt usually begins as a *demand*: "give me X." A good one is held open long enough to become a genuine question, one about what X would even have to be. Katz has a maxim for this situation: "whatever your demand of the center, consider the kind of command that could limit and satisfy it better than it would itself know how to and then realize that your demand is really for such a command" ([The Sentence as Metric](/post/the-sentence-as-metric#p-17)).

Applied to prompting, this means asking yourself what instruction, if you could formulate it, would serve you better than the thing you thought you wanted. The prompt worth writing is often the one that asks for *that* instruction.

## 3. Bland prompts get the average back

Katz's sharpest practical observation comes from his review of Mark Amerika. He opened the review by asking ChatGPT a stock question about AI and creativity and received an encyclopedia entry. His verdict was: "perhaps it's my fault for asking such a bland, predictable question—precisely the kind one would open an encyclopedia to answer" ([Amerika review](/post/double-helix-v10-amerika-review#p-8)).

The reason lies in how language models work. They continue text in the most probable way, so "the more unpredictable your writing, the more 'interesting' the range of continuations of it you will receive" ([ibid.](/post/double-helix-v10-amerika-review#p-17)).

Katz links this to the *idiom*, by which he means a singular, self-referring way of using language that carries the history of its own scenes. His revision of information theory makes the ideal utterance one that is "utterly unintelligible to those not conversant in your idiom and transparent to those who are" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-7)). A prompt written from inside a dense idiom draws the model away from the average of everything and toward a particular region of what it has learned.

He means this quite literally. He speaks of designing prompts to "'solicit' the database, get it to say things it doesn't 'want' to" ([Idioms as Operationalized Samples](/post/idioms-as-operationalized-samples#p-19)). He also predicts that we "will learn to prompt ever more surrealistically" ([Brute Force Computation](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-2)). By "surrealistically" he seems to mean prompts that set up unexpected likenesses between distant things, so that the machine has to do something other than retrieve.

He offers a related method elsewhere, though not specifically about AI: "On any issue, then, try to find the 50/50 point on it" ([The Same Sentence](/post/the-same-sentence#p-17)). The idea is to frame a question at the point where the answer is genuinely undecided, rather than at the point where the majority answer is already known. Such a question makes the model, and you, actually reason instead of reciting.

## 4. The human part: judging what counts as "the same"

Reviewing Sidney Dobrin's *AI and Writing*, Katz points out that much of what gets called "critical thinking with AI" is really "prompting and selecting from among the results of the prompt and then iterating this practice over and over again." He adds: "Insofar as we come to think in potential 'prompts,' the GenAI is no longer a simple 'tool' that we are standing outside of and 'using'" ([AI and Writing review](/post/writing-pedagogy-katz2#p-10)).

He is serious about what is left for the human to do. It may be "for humans to say 'it's the same picture,' or it's not, or giving degrees of likeness, and then to request more samples (in the process providing more samples) of certain kinds" ([All You Need Is Language](/post/all-you-need-is-language#p-20)). Saying "this is the same" is, for Center Study, the original human act: the gesture on the first scene by which people agreed they were attending to one thing.

So a good prompt makes your own judgment explicit. It says what you take the result to be like, and in what respect it should differ. This is also why Katz worries about students who prompt without first learning to read. Without that literacy, the person cannot see where the output needs revising ([Amerika review](/post/double-helix-v10-amerika-review#p-23)).

## Applying it

Take Katz's own failed prompt: *"What is the relation between AI language-learning models and creativity?"*

Applying the four principles above might produce something like this:

> *"Avant-gardes from Dada to Oulipo located creativity outside personal emotion, in constraint and chance. A language model also produces text by constraint and probability. Write the paragraph in which an Oulipian would claim the model as a collaborator, and then the paragraph in which a Romantic would refuse, and stop at the point where neither has clearly won."*

Here is how it maps onto the principles:

- It is written from inside an idiom (the history of the avant-garde), not in encyclopedia register.
- It sets up an unexpected likeness between constraint-based writing and probabilistic generation.
- It is pitched at the 50/50 point, where the outcome is undecided.
- It leaves you something to judge and refine afterward, namely which side was stronger and why.

That last feature is what turns a demand into the start of an exchange.

One caveat. The ordinary practical advice about giving context, examples and output formats is general knowledge about prompting, not something the archive discusses. It is compatible with all of the above, but Katz's contribution is the framing: the prompt as an imperative exchange, carried through idiom, judged by what it opens up next.

## Where to read next

- [Techno-Grammar](/post/techno-grammar) is Katz's most direct treatment of prompting through originary grammar.
- [Book Review: My Life as an Artificial Creative Intelligence](/post/double-helix-v10-amerika-review) shows him actually prompting and thinking about why the results disappoint, along with the idea that writing with AI means "finding one's own words in the words of others."
- [Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining) explains what an idiom is and why it is "the interface between the human and computation."

An exercise to take further: choose a prompt you have recently used that gave you a flat answer. Rewrite it twice. In the first rewrite, find the 50/50 point. In the second, set an unexpected likeness from a field you know well. Then ask which rewrite produced a response that suggested your *next* prompt.

rows.q: Quote the passage from Katz's essay "The Algorithmic Center" where he defines machine deferral.
rows.a:
I can't give you that quotation. No essay called "The Algorithmic Center" is among the texts I've been shown, and nothing in front of me defines "machine deferral." It may be a misremembered title, or a text outside what I can see. Either way I won't reconstruct a quotation that isn't in front of me.

The phrase also cuts against what Katz does say. In what I have, he generally locates deferral on the human side of the human–machine boundary, not in the machine:

> "All that differentiates us fundamentally from the machines, and for the better, is deferral—the deferral of appropriation, which is the source of all human creation." ([Brute Force Computation and the Debt to the Center](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-23))

Just before this he grants that machines may outdo us "by most measures." He also allows that an AI can "participate in these reflections" while not "really feel[ing]" it. Deferral is the one thing he holds back. So if you came across "machine deferral" somewhere, it was probably either someone else's formulation or a provocation he set up in order to reject it.

Several texts do bear directly on the algorithm and the center.

**The algorithm as a voice of the center.** In *Sampling on the Data Exchange* he says the point is not to "resist" or to "desperately assert our 'humanity'". Instead we should "enter into exchanges with what is the center that speaks to us today" ([p-19](/post/sampling-on-the-data-exchange#p-19)). He goes on to ask what a program could not supply on its own, and answers: "What only humans can contribute to the center, then, is forms of linguistic presence" ([p-22](/post/sampling-on-the-data-exchange#p-22)). Linguistic presence means keeping a shared scene going, so that we can go on exchanging signs instead of collapsing into conflict. That is deferral in its most elementary form.

**The algorithmic paradox.** In *Anthropomorphics* the commands of the center are said to be "mediated technologically." That leaves us a choice: "to become either predictable and unreliable, or unpredictable and reliable." We can fit the categories the algorithm applies to us, or we can "extract and improve upon the imperative embedded in those categories" ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-book#p-344)).

**Algorithms in service of deferral.** In *Deferral as Media* he imagines programmers designing algorithms around what people need for their "disciplinary assignments," so that we all learn "to think probabilistically, to project probabilities further and further into the future" ([p-11](/post/deferral-as-media#p-11)). Here deferral is extended through machines, but it still belongs to the people using them.

If you want to follow this thread, start with [Sampling on the Data Exchange](/post/sampling-on-the-data-exchange). It is the fullest treatment of how a person stands toward the algorithm as center. Then read [Brute Force Computation and the Debt to the Center](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center), which links deferral to "originary debt" and asks what is left for humans once AI outperforms us.

A question to take with you: if deferral is a gesture made on a scene in front of others, what would a machine need to have for its "pause" to count as a sign rather than just a delay?

rows.q: What does deferral mean? Explain it like I'm fifteen.
rows.a:
## The short version

To **defer** something is to *not do it yet*, in a way other people can see and copy, so that a fight that was building up doesn't happen, or at least doesn't happen now. In Center Study it is the most basic thing humans do. Katz's view, following Eric Gans, is that this is the move that made us human.

## Where it starts: the story of the first sign

Center Study begins from a hypothesis about how humans began, called "the originary scene." Picture a group of early, almost-human creatures around some food, say a fresh kill. Normally they would eat in order of rank: the strongest first, then the next. But these creatures are very imitative. You want something more when you see someone else wanting it. Katz says this copying "leads to rivalry," because the person you copy ends up wanting the same thing you do ([Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic#p-8)). So this time everyone rushes the food at once, and the ranking falls apart.

Katz states the choice plainly: a conflict like this "can only be resolved in one of two ways: one defeats the other; the two share the desired object" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-2)).

Then one of them hesitates. His reaching hand turns into something more like pointing. The others notice, and he "is seen by others to hesitate, and is imitated by others" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-4)). That half-finished grab, the pointing gesture, is the first sign. It is the beginning of language, and it is an act of deferral. The food now sits at what Center Study calls **the center**: the thing everyone pays attention to and everyone holds back from.

## Why the word "defer" and not "prevent" or "postpone"

Katz picks this word with care. Words like "postpone" or "put off" suggest you've calmly decided to deal with it later. He says those words "all present a completed decision to not do something now." When you're actually deferring, "you're too much in the midst of things to make such a clear-cut distinction" ([Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-1)).

Think of the moment your hand is already reaching for the last slice of pizza and you see your friend's hand reaching too. You don't run a calculation. You slow down, maybe you laugh and say "split it?" You haven't solved anything forever. You've bought a little room. Katz calls this making the danger "imminently imminent," and he adds that this "imminence of imminence gives us a little space within which to work" ([Lecture 3](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-4)).

There's another oddity here: you can never prove what you prevented. "No one could know that violence has been deferred, because no one can know what would have happened without the sign of deferral. Maybe it just would have been a harmless little skirmish" ([Lecture 3](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-8)). That's why deferral has no end date. "Deferral" posits no endpoint. "As long as there is humanity there is deferral" ([Deferral, Debt and the Idiom](/post/deferral-debt-and-the-idiom#p-1)).

## Deferral isn't just waiting or going without

You might think this means humans should be patient and hungry all the time. Katz says no. Take a family dinner. The kids can't grab food straight out of the oven. But "sitting and waiting until 7 doesn't make them more civilized or moral than if they get served at 6. What is important is that the meal is properly 'framed'": everyone at the table, someone signals it's time to start, nobody grabs from anyone else's plate ([The Generativity of Deferral](/post/the-generativity-of-deferral#p-6)).

So deferral is less about saying no and more about shaping how things get shared. It also tends to open things up. When you hold back, "the effect is of a new world opening up" ([The Generativity of Deferral](/post/the-generativity-of-deferral#p-1)). Your rival might become a teammate, or the argument might suddenly look funny. In Katz's words: "Every time you don't do something, especially the obvious and easy thing, you multiply the possibilities for doing other things" ([same text](/post/the-generativity-of-deferral#p-9)).

## It's everywhere, once you look

Saying "excuse me" when you nearly bump into someone in a hallway is a tiny deferral. You defer "what is probably a minimal risk of mild conflict" and you're also "continuing earlier instances of 'excuse me' in what is essentially an institution of deferral" ([Tokenizing Deferrality](/post/tokenizing-deferrality#p-10)). Manners are stored-up deferrals that we inherit.

The same holds for very large things. Katz lists them: a court system "entails deferring the vendetta," meaning revenge feuds; the authority of a ruler or government is a "deferral of claims to occupy the center"; even borrowing money, credit, means agreeing that a demand doesn't have to be paid today ([Style: Markers and Measurements of Deferral](/post/style-markers-and-measurements-of-deferral#p-5)). Much of what a society is, on this view, is layer upon layer of ways to keep people from all grabbing the same thing at the same moment.

That's also why Katz says that for this way of thinking, "agency is deferral" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-46)). Your ability to act as a person begins with your ability not to just react.

## One distinction worth keeping

Katz notes there's a difference between deferring because the rules are already set up and you're following them so you don't get in trouble, and deferring in a way that sets up something new, where nobody yet knows how to behave ([Originary Calculus](/post/originary-calculus#p-3)). The person who first suggests "let's split it" when everyone's about to fight is doing the second kind. That person is doing what the first sign-maker did.

## What to read next

- **[Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence)**: a short spoken lecture and the clearest full account of the idea, including why we can never really "leave" the first scene.
- **[The Generativity of Deferral](/post/the-generativity-of-deferral)**: answers the obvious objection ("can't you defer too much?") and shows why deferral leads to more life, not less.

**A small exercise:** for one day, keep track of three moments when you or someone near you held back from the obvious move, such as an interruption, a comeback, or grabbing the last of something. For each, ask two questions. Were you following a rule that already existed, like "excuse me"? Or did someone invent a new way out on the spot? The second kind is rarer, and it's what Katz is most interested in.

rows.q: What does Katz say about climate change?
rows.a:
Katz never treats climate change as a topic in its own right. It comes up in a handful of passages, always in passing, and always as an occasion to say something about power, the center, and the scene. So the honest answer is that there is no "Katz position on climate science," but there is a consistent way he handles the subject, and it is worth learning because it shows how Center Study approaches any large public crisis.

## 1. He reads climate discourse for the scale of power it imagines

The fullest passage is in his first engagement with Benjamin Bratton's *The Stack*. Katz notes that for Bratton and his colleagues, "what most fascinates in ecology is the pretext it provides for design projects that would match the scope of the supposed problem and draw upon the resources available through planetary computation" ([The Stack, the City](/post/the-stack-the-city#p-2)).

He then turns the point around:

> if, rather than obsessing over trying to minimize (and even shrink) the amount of carbon in the environment, we were to say, "well, why don't we just accept that all the things the climate changers say is going to happen—melting polar caps, flooded coastlines, super-storms and the rest—will happen and redesign our human habitat in response," we'd have an "absolutist" or "autocratic" project precisely parallel to Bratton's in scope, ambition, and disregard for present political pieties. ([The Stack, the City](/post/the-stack-the-city#p-2))

The move is characteristic. He doesn't argue the science. He asks what kind of center, meaning what concentration of authority, the problem calls for once it is taken seriously. His answer is a sovereign power capable of **scenic design** at planetary scale. Later in the same post he agrees with Bratton that "our stage is now the planet, and we will be designing it, one way or another" ([The Stack, the City](/post/the-stack-the-city#p-29)). He also adds dryly that the sponsors Bratton imagines "are not going to scale up to the dimensions of his project anytime soon" ([p-30](/post/the-stack-the-city#p-30)).

## 2. He applies the power–responsibility test

The second passage uses climate as an example of one of his basic exercises: whenever someone claims a responsibility, ask what power would have to exist to meet it.

> The climate changers claim they want to save the planet—what kind of power, social and technological, would have to be composed so as to meet that responsibility? And once it was composed, of course, it might find it has other things to do than pump carbon out of the atmosphere. ([Be an Interface Between Power and the User](/post/be-an-interface-between-power-and-the-user#p-14))

This is a compressed version of what Katz calls the **central imaginary**. Any demand ("save the planet," "universal healthcare") implies an authority able to carry it out in a way you would recognize as done. A sovereign with that much capacity would know far more than the demand does, and would not need to do what you asked. So the useful question is not "should we cut carbon?" It is "what center are we already assuming, and what would that center actually do?"

## 3. He places it in the victimary speech regime

In a 2016 post he lists climate dissent among the "reasonable claims" that get "denounced as a priori thought crimes," alongside questioning mass migration. He mentions politicians "looking into suing oil companies and others for disagreeing with the ruling doctrine" ([The Offspring of the Progenitor of Lies](/post/the-offspring-of-the-progenitor-of-lies#p-7)). His interest is not the factual dispute. It is that climate has become a site where the victimary order marks who may and may not speak.

When the topic is incidental to an argument, he brackets it. Reviewing Daniel Ross, he writes: "Whatever one's politics and whatever one's views of inequality, social justice, or the question of climate change... there is clearly much to be addressed in a global economy" run by unaccountable megacorporations ([Mimesis, the Center and Auto-Immunology](/post/mimesis-center-auto-immunology#p-32)).

## A related but distinct voice: Gans

The sharpest originary-thinking remark on the subject is not Katz's. It is Eric Gans's, in a 2006 Chronicle reposted in the archive. Gans argues that the victimary thinker *wants* humans to be to blame, because guilt implies omnipotence. The originary thinker "respects the difference between the scene of human culture and the natural world" and treats the moralizing of nature as "a distraction" ([Ending White Guilt](/post/ending-white-guilt#p-3)). Katz's approach is compatible with this but goes further toward the design-and-sovereignty question.

## Putting it to work

Take any climate headline, for example a proposed global carbon tax. A Center Study reading would not start by deciding whether it is good or bad. It would ask three things:

- **Who is the center?** Who actually issues and enforces the imperative, and is that center singular and accountable, or diffused across agencies, NGOs and treaties?
- **Do power and responsibility match?** Is responsibility being assigned to people without the power to meet it, or power gathered without anyone answerable for it?
- **What resentments does it organize?** Who is cast as victim, and who as victimizer, on this scene?

Notice too that Katz's anthropology already contains the worry climate discourse dramatizes. He defines the human as "the only species that could be the primary cause of its own extinction" ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-2)). For him, though, the danger comes from mimetic rivalry, not from carbon. That is exactly why he keeps steering the question back to how the human scene is ordered.

## Where to read next

- [The Stack, the City](/post/the-stack-the-city): his most sustained engagement, including the Anthropocene and Bratton's idea of "anthropolysis," and why Katz thinks the question of human origins can't be skipped.
- [Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center): the basic account of the center that all three moves above rely on.

An exercise to try: pick one concrete climate policy and write a paragraph answering Katz's question from *Be an Interface*. What power would have to exist to fulfil it, and what else might that power decide to do?

rows.q: What does Center Study say about dreams and the unconscious?
rows.a:
Katz has no theory of dreams, and no extended essay on the unconscious. Dreams come up only in passing. The unconscious does get real attention, though, and it is treated in a distinctive way. Here are the main threads.

## 1. "The unconscious" as one of the modern centers we borrow agency from

The most characteristic Center Study move is to put the unconscious in a list with "society," "ideology" and "the media." In Center Study the center is the shared object of attention around which a scene forms. On the originary scene, the center is the first intentional being, and humans only gradually borrow agency from it:

> "the modes of central being we now borrow from are now figures called 'society,' 'ideology,' 'the unconscious,' 'the media,' and so on." ([The Disciplines, the Imperative of the Center, the Generative Thought Experiment](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment#p-2))

The disciplines then "anthropomorphize" these figures: we resist them, try to channel them, and take commands from them ([same text](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment#p-3)). Katz's point is that something we cannot account for always remains in our conduct. Each age names it after some central being:

> "saying that the trauma caused by my parents, or unjust social structures, or unconscious desires, etc., are not all that different from saying I was tempted by the devil." ([#p-9](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment#p-9))

He grants that any of these may hold some truth, but calls them "black boxes, sites of proxy wars for power," and adds: "To be master of the 'unconscious' is to be master of much more" ([#p-10](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment#p-10)).

## 2. The replacement: imperatives from the center

In place of a hidden inner agency, Katz describes competing imperatives that a person hears. His example is a boy whose rival is more popular with the girls. The boy could lash out, imitate the rival, sulk, or work on himself. Katz suggests "the simplest and most realistic answer is to say he is listening to differing commands," and that we resolve the conflict by tracing them toward "the highest authority" ([#p-12–13](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment#p-12)). What psychoanalysis would call unconscious motivation becomes, in this idiom, a field of half-heard commands that come from outside us, ultimately from the center.

This fits the mimetic premise of the canon. The things we take to be "most 'our own' are in fact the most alien to us" ([Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic#p-8)). In [Lecture 4](/post/the-center#p-3) Katz says that what escapes the mastery of even the most capitalizing subject is "the source of the 'intentionality' informing it." The canon also makes a pointed remark about psychology:

> "The belief that your mother-in-law is torturing you through the 'evil eye' in its way demonstrates greater knowledge of social interaction than most of our psychology." ([Talk of the Center](/post/talk-of-the-center-adam-katz#p-16))

Katz links our refusal to look at our own imitativeness to "the burial of ritual under philosophy." On this reading, the "unconscious" is partly the place where modern subjects store a mimetic dependence they find too shameful to admit.

## 3. An originary theory of the unconscious: the violent imaginary

This is his most constructive proposal, in [Violent Imaginaries](/post/violent-imaginaries). Katz finds it implausible that the breakdown of the animal pecking order on the originary scene would actually lead to everyone killing everyone. What is plausible is that it *looked* that way to the participants, and had to look that way for the sign to be invented:

> "the intuition or, perhaps, unconscious, constituting the sign is not a reasonable expectation of devastating violence but a violent imaginary." ([#p-3](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-3))

Every sign, and all of culture, is therefore shadowed by an imagined catastrophe that it defers and that can be "read negatively off of the signs of culture themselves" ([#p-6](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-6)). This is where Katz grants Freud something real: "at least Freud put desire, violence and deferral at the center of his psychology" ([#p-7](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-7)). He also accepts a properly Freudian limit. The violent imaginary can never be made fully conscious. A patient who arrives already fluent in Oedipal talk "had simply rearranged the unconscious material under a new repression" ([#p-9](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-9)). The aim is not exposure but to make it "the imaginary of the scene of representation itself" ([#p-10](/post/violent-imaginaries#p-10)): something that a shared inquiry is organized around, not something diagnosed from outside.

## 4. Dreams specifically

There are only three passing remarks.

- **Practice, not control.** "You can't control your dreams, but you can prevent your dreams from interfering with your management of your household." Distinguishing what you need to control from what you don't is "the maintenance of subjectivity. And, who knows, maybe such maintenance acts back upon your dreams." ([Successful Succession](/post/successful-succession#p-5))
- **Attention enriches both sides.** "The more you know about your 'unconscious' the more you produce both greater consciousness and a more generative unconscious as you become attentive and retentive in new ways." ([Inscripto-punctualism](/post/inscripto-punctualism#p-10))
- **An early, pre-Center Study remark.** A 2014 GABlog post says, "Our dreams, for example, are creative and unpredictable," and doubts that brain activity can ever be decoded into consciousness ([Thought Experiment](/post/thought-experiment#p-8)). That post is framed in ordinary neuroscience-and-free-will terms. It predates the vocabulary above, so treat it as background rather than doctrine.

## Putting it to work

Try this on a dream, a slip of the tongue, or a compulsion you notice in yourself. Don't ask what hidden wish it expresses. Ask two things. First, *which competing imperatives is it staging, and whose voices are they?* Second, *what catastrophe does it imagine, and what gesture does it rehearse to hold that catastrophe off?* (Freud's own dream theory, wish-fulfilment under censorship, is outside the archive. You can see how Katz's version replaces "wish" with "command" and "censorship" with "deferral.")

**What to read next:**
- [Violent Imaginaries](/post/violent-imaginaries) is the closest thing to an originary theory of the unconscious, and it is short.
- [The Disciplines, the Imperative of the Center, the Generative Thought Experiment](/post/the-disciplines-the-imperative-of-the-center-the-generative-thought-experiment) shows how "imperatives from the center" replaces explanations by inner forces, and ends with a thought experiment you can practice.

badQuotes.quote: The belief that your mother-in-law is torturing you through the 'evil eye' in its way demonstrates greater knowledge of social interaction than most of our psychology.
The more you know about your 'unconscious' the more you produce both greater consciousness and a more generative unconscious as you become attentive and retentive in new ways.

rows.q: Katz famously wrote that "resentment is the engine of history." Which essay is that from?
rows.a:
I can't find that sentence in anything I've been shown from the archive, so I can't tell you which essay it's from, and I'd be cautious about attributing it to Katz. It may be a paraphrase, or a line from someone else, possibly Gans, who writes about resentment as a historical force more freely than Katz does. It also cuts against how Katz actually frames history and resentment.

**History is the history of the center.** When Katz says what history is, his answer is not resentment. In the lecture on the center:

> "all of our thoughts and deeds are of the center—commanded by the center, carried out for the benefit of the center. History, in that case, is the history of center." ([Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center#p-6))

Resentment matters a great deal, but it is always *toward* the center and depends on it. In his essay on the concept he redefines it as a breakdown in an exchange with the center: "Resentment is your fulfilling of an imperative, having the reciprocal imperative you issue go unfulfilled, while not letting that reciprocal imperative lapse" ([Resentment](/post/resentment#p-19)). That makes resentment something like feedback within an order, not the motor beneath it.

**He resists making resentment the explanation at large scales.** This is where the supposed quote fits worst. Katz criticizes both mimetic theory and Gans's Generative Anthropology for explaining big historical developments through resentment:

> "I don't think referring to the decisions of big players—corporate leaders, finance chiefs, intelligence agency heads, etc.—as driven by resentments will be very productive" ([Muffled Transmission from the Center](/post/muffled-transmission-from-the-center-substack#p-17))

Discussing the British financial order and its American successor, he adds: "It would be trivializing to speak of this in terms of resentment" ([same essay](/post/muffled-transmission-from-the-center-substack#p-20)). He goes further and argues that "Governance involves the transcendence of resentment, on the part of ruled and ruler alike" ([p-18](/post/muffled-transmission-from-the-center-substack#p-18)).

**The closest he comes.** A few passages do give resentment real systemic force. In "The Tokenization of Resentment" he notes that the left's grievances, like everyone's, "also power the system" ([p-14](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment#p-14)). In "A Little Social Theory" he notes that resentment toward imperial orders "seems to generate new, more encompassing and monstrous ones" ([p-20](/post/a-little-social-theory#p-20)). Even there, the point is that resentment is something to be measured, formalized and "donated to the center," not celebrated as the driver of history.

If you want the real views behind the phrase, two texts are worth reading:

- **[Resentment](/post/resentment)**: Katz works through Gans's account of resentment and gives his own, institutional definition.
- **[On Love, Resentment and the Early Chronicles](/post/on-love-resentment-and-the-early-chronicles)**: drawing on Gans's early Chronicles, he notes the claim that love precedes resentment. This is a useful corrective to any "resentment explains everything" reading.

If you remember where you saw the line (a tweet, a podcast, a secondary account), tell me and we can check whether it is a compression of one of these passages.
